full_text:
Queen Zubaydah, the celebrated consort of Caliph Harun al-Rashid, was renowned not only for her royal elegance, but for an architectural vision and public benevolence that outshone all the monarchs of her era.

During her pilgrimage to the holy city of Mecca, the queen was deeply moved by the hardships endured by the poor pilgrims. The desert heat was scorching, the mountain passes were treacherous, and water was so scarce that a single waterskin cost more than a poor traveler’s entire savings. Thousands of men, women, and children suffered agonizing thirst on the desert roads.

Standing upon the arid plains of Arafat, Queen Zubaydah summoned her chief engineers, geologists, and architects. She declared with royal resolve: 'I will not see the pilgrims of the earth thirst in this valley. I command you to cut through the solid granite mountains, divert the distant springs of the hills, and construct an aqueduct that shall bring fresh, sweet water to every corner of Mecca!'

Her chief treasurer stepped forward in alarm: 'My Queen, to cut through these mountains and build stone aqueducts across forty miles of desert will exhaust our imperial treasury; it will cost millions of gold dinars!'

Queen Zubaydah removed her pearl necklace and said with majestic calm: 'Build the aqueduct, even if every blow of the iron chisel costs a gold dinar! The gold of monarchs turns to dust, but the water that refreshes a thirsty traveler flows as a blessing before the throne of heaven forever.'

For ten years, thousands of stonemasons chiseled through stone, built underground qanats, vaulted reservoirs, and arched aqueducts. The waters of Ayn Zubaydah flowed in abundance, filling fountains, wells, and cisterns for over a thousand years, immortalizing the queen’s name as the mother of the pilgrims.
moral: True royal magnificence is measured by public works that relieve the suffering of millions of travelers.
